seo.title: Karmic tail 9 3 12 compatibility: a garden for two hermits
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 3 12 compatibility: a couple withdraws from the world, grows a garden of its own and risks hanging in it. The cards, the maths and Goethe.

title: The 9-3-12 karmic tail in compatibility: a couple who planted a garden for two
short: The Hermit, The Empress and The Hanged Man: a card of solitude, a card of abundance and a card of a man hanging upside down. In the couple's karmic tail 9-3-12 these three cards add up to a story many couples recognise. The pair enters its task wanting to close the door on the world and be alone together. It lives the task through everything it grows together: a home, a garden, children, a shared business. And its main task is a single one: not to hang in its own garden, not to turn a shared life into a quiet mutual sacrifice in which each waits for a sign instead of speaking and choosing.

sections.h2: A novel that begins with a garden for two
paragraphs: Edward and Charlotte loved each other when they were young, but other people's calculations parted them. His father married him off to a rich older lady; Charlotte had to give her hand to a man she respected but did not love. Both were widowed, met again and married late, after long waiting. Charlotte herself describes how they arranged their life. Her daughter and her niece were sent away to school, "merely that we might have our own lives to ourselves". She took the house, he took everything outside. In the evenings he plays the flute and she the piano. He was going to read his travel journals to her, so that the two of them could "travel over in recollection the world which we were unable to see together". Quotations from the novel follow the translation by James Anthony Froude and R. Dillon Boylan.

The main conversation of the first chapter takes place in that very hut. Edward remarks that it is rather small. "It is large enough for you and me, at any rate," Charlotte answers. "There is room for a third, too, easily." "Of course; and for a fourth also." They are talking about Edward's friend the Captain, who is out of work and whom Edward wants to invite to the estate. Charlotte is against it. Then Edward asks the question that holds the whole entry of this tail: "All the work we have done — I in the garden, you in the park — is it all only for a pair of hermits?" Goethe's German has the word Einsiedler, hermits.

Charlotte answers with a premonition. "Nothing is of greater moment, in any state of things, than the intervention of a third person," she says: she has seen friends, lovers, husbands and wives "whose whole moral condition has been inverted by it". The German word is umgekehrt, turned upside down. The man turned upside down is the twelfth card, the main task of the tail. The first chapter runs through 9-3-12 from beginning to end: two hermits, the garden they have grown and a foreboding of the overturn.

The novel is a mirror, not a forecast. In Goethe, the emptiness between two people is filled by people: the Captain and young Ottilie, Charlotte's niece. The 9-3-12 tail promises a couple neither a third nor a fourth. In real couples the emptiness is more often filled by things to do: renovations, a country house, children, work, a business. The mechanism stays the same.

sections.h2: The Hermit at the entry: a common language of silence
paragraphs: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a "common language". With The Hermit in this place, couples recognise themselves at once. They are happy together and do not much need guests. Friends hear the news after the fact: they have moved, married, changed jobs. Each can be alone in the next room, and this is not coldness but an agreement. Love is shown in deeds rather than words, and every step is taken slowly, from the first kiss to the wedding.

Goethe has a scene that shows the reverse side of this entry. Edward is reading aloud, Charlotte happens to glance at his page, and he flares up: "When anybody looks over my book, I always feel as if I were being torn in two." A Hermit couple shares a silence for two, but inside each of them there is another, private one, and it is guarded just as jealously.

Benebell Wen offers two readings of the Hermit's lantern. It is "the shining of light in the darkness for others". And it may represent "someone who sees the world through his or her own light". Both live at the entry of this couple's tail. While the two shine for each other, silence is their common language. When there are two lanterns and each looks its own way, the common language of silence turns into two silences.

The entry sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can become resistance. In the novel this happens literally. The hut built for "you and me" soon becomes the place where the four of them sit together for the first time. And later it becomes the place Charlotte runs to alone: "she flung herself into the narrow room in the little hermitage" and gave way to a despair she had not imagined a moment before. Solitude for two has become solitude for one. This is how the weak entry looks in a 9-3-12 couple: the unsaid gets stored in the shared silence — hurt, tiredness, doubt — until being together is uncomfortable and parting is frightening.

sections.h2: The Empress in the middle: everything that grows faster than conversation
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple lives the way from the wish to the task. In Lisovskaya this point has no meaning of its own: it adds to the main task. Our reading is the road the couple travels. In 9-3-12 that road is The Empress: growth, fertility, the home, everything that can be planted and raised.

That is exactly what happens in the novel. The Captain arrives and at once finds work: he surveys the estate, lays out paths, runs the building. Charlotte sends for Ottilie because her housekeeper is leaving, and the girl is given the house to run. Both people the couple let into its world were let in by the household. From here the novel turns for a long stretch into a book about landscape gardening: a new house on the hill, the laying of a foundation stone, fireworks over the water. The great project is to join three ponds into one lake. The Captain has his doubts: "in more than one sense, it seemed a very questionable proceeding". But the work has already begun.

The Empress is generous with coincidences too. Edward asks that his planes by the middle pond be spared: "those trees I planted myself". How long have they been there, Ottilie asks. "Just about as long as you have been in the world." Later he finds in his father's diaries that the day and year of the planting were the day and year of her birth. Whatever is planted will one day mean more than anyone intended.

Wen calls The Empress "the card of fruition" and adds at once that it "might also be a foreshadowing of unintended or unanticipated consequences affecting that fruition". The lake made for the sake of the view becomes, in Goethe, the scene of the novel's great disaster. And one more scene. Edward and Charlotte have a son. At the christening Ottilie sees her own eyes in the baby's face, and Mittler, the family friend, sees "a most striking likeness to the Captain". The child resembles the people his parents thought about and kept silent about. Goethe made literal what in a 9-3-12 couple usually happens quietly: **the unsaid grows into what the two create together.** Not in children, but in the tone of the house, in the way daily life is arranged, in where the strength and money go.

A strong Empress in the middle is a couple for whom everything grows: the home is lived in, the shared table is generous, each has work of their own, and one partner's growth does not outrun the other's. A weak one is building work that never ends, because while it goes on nobody has to talk about the main thing. The renovation drags into its third year, a country house is added to it, a new project to the country house, and each job honestly fills an evening that might have been spent talking.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man: a marriage left hanging
paragraphs: The couple's main task is its main difficulty, and it is read above all through what does not work. The second part of the novel is suspension from start to finish. Edward goes off to war. At the foundation-stone ceremony a glass engraved with initials was thrown into the air, caught and not broken, and Edward took it for an omen; now he decides: "I will put myself in the place of this glass, and it shall be an omen whether our union be possible or not." Charlotte stays behind to wait and gives up her own feeling for the Captain. Ottilie takes a vow of silence and nearly stops eating. In a letter she admits: "Too literally, perhaps, I have observed my promise," and asks: "leave me to my own inward self." The marriage is neither lived nor dissolved. It hangs.

The voice of society stands over this marriage. Mittler, whose very name means "mediator", reconciles other people's families and makes a speech about marriage: "It is an infinite debt, which can only be discharged through all eternity"; it has its annoyances, "and it is as it should be". At the end of the novel Edward tells his friend a sentence that sounds like a verdict on all this suspension: "genius is required for everything; for martyrdom as well as the rest." He sees that his sacrifice is an imitation of someone else's.

The books say the same. Waite writes that The Hanged Man "has been called falsely a card of martyrdom". Wen, describing the reversed card, warns the Seeker "not to confuse martyrdom with selfishness" and names the trap of being "preoccupied with appearing holy". In life it looks ordinary. She does not go to her class reunion "because there's so much to do at home". He turns down a job in another city "because of the family". Nobody asked for these sacrifices, and nobody knows they were made. A few years later they are presented for payment — as reproach, as tiredness, as silence at dinner. One partner holds the relationship together with the last of their strength and hears reproaches in return, yet cannot leave. Outside there is a pretty picture, inside it is heavy, and decisions are made "because that's how it should be".

The most exact words about the main task of 9-3-12 are spoken by Charlotte herself, when it is too late: "I ought to have made up my mind to it before." From the first chapter Edward proposes to "draw lots", and she answers that "in such a serious matter, this seems almost a crime". Yet for the whole novel the four of them wait for a sign: a glass, a coincidence of dates, chance. **The Hanged Man in the main task is exactly this: waiting for a sign.** What the couple has to learn is not patience but how to stop hanging.

sections.h2: What Waite writes: a tree that grew in the garden
paragraphs: In Waite, The Empress sits before a field of ripening corn with a fall of water behind her, and he sums her up as "universal fecundity". The Hanged Man hangs from a tree, and Waite is careful to point out three things: "the tree of sacrifice is living wood, with leaves thereon"; "the face expresses deep entrancement, not suffering"; and the figure as a whole "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death".

Put side by side, these two cards give a picture of the tail. The Hanged Man's tree grows where The Empress keeps house. **In 9-3-12 a person hangs not from a gallows but from what they have grown themselves**: the home, the shared business, the duty to the family. That is also the key to the way out. A living tree does not need to be cut down. One can do with it what The Hanged Man himself does: look at the world from the other side while hanging. Wen describes this card as "seeing the same issues as others, but through a different perspective".

Waite ends his account of The Hanged Man with "intimations concerning a great awakening that is possible". Goethe's novel ends in a chapel where Edward and Ottilie lie buried side by side: "So lie the lovers, sleeping side by side… and what a happy moment that will be when one day they wake again together!" Goethe put the awakening off beyond life, and not only for those two: Charlotte is left without them, among her park and her lake. The task of a 9-3-12 couple is to wake up while alive.

sections.h2: Choice or necessity: what sits at the centre of such a couple
paragraphs: The key piece of evidence is the novel's title. Wahlverwandtschaften, "elective affinities", is an eighteenth-century chemical term. In 1775 the Swedish chemist Torbern Bergman called his treatise "De attractionibus electivis" — "On Elective Attractions". In the fourth chapter the Captain explains the term to Charlotte. Limestone placed in diluted sulphuric acid combines with it and becomes gypsum, while its former companion, the gaseous acid, flies off. "It really looks as if one relation had been deliberately chosen in preference to another." Charlotte disagrees: "I cannot see any choice in this; I see a natural necessity rather, and scarcely that. After all, it is perhaps merely a case of opportunity. Opportunity makes relations as it makes thieves."

Both cards that can stand at the centre of a 9-3-12 couple are present in this argument. The centre is the shared atmosphere, what lies inside the couple and is not on show. In 62.7% of such couples it is The Devil, in 37.3% The Lovers. The Lovers is the card of choice, and the first word in Waite's divinatory list for it is "Attraction" — the same word as in Bergman's title. Waite's Devil is "fatality", with the proviso that follows at once: "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". **Choice and necessity: the two words the argument over Goethe's title turns on, and the two cards the centre chooses between.**
Our run of the site's engine over every date since 1900 shows what decides which card takes the centre. The 9-3-12 tail is formed by two combinations of the partners' personal tails:

And here is the curious part: the other card does not vanish. The 6-8-20 tail begins with The Lovers, the 15-20-5 tail with The Devil. **Every 9-3-12 couple holds both choice and necessity**: one of the two cards sits at the centre of the couple, the other at the entry of one partner's personal tail.

One more detail from Goethe's chemistry. Opposite substances, the Captain says, reach out for each other, "modify each other's character, and form in connection an entirely new substance". No personal chart has 15 at its centre: no individual ever has The Devil there. It appears only when two are combined, just as gypsum appears only where lime has met the acid. What such a couple experiences as "it just turned out that way" or "we got pulled in" belongs neither to him nor to her, but to the compound they make.

Charlotte gives the answer in the same chapter. Man "is raised very many steps above these elements; and if he has been somewhat liberal with such fine words as Election and Elective Affinities, he will do well to turn back again into himself, and take the opportunity of considering carefully the value and meaning of such expressions". This is The Hermit in his strong form: solitude not to hide but to stop and think before calling a decision fate. At the end of the novel Charlotte walks this road herself. First she speaks of "certain things on which destiny obstinately insists", and then she breaks off: "And, indeed, what am I saying? It is but my own desire, my own purpose, against which I acted so unthinkingly, which destiny is again bringing in my way." What looked like fate turned out to be a choice nobody had spoken aloud.

sections.h2: How this tail looks in the calculation
paragraphs: An example is the couple born 17.01.1976 and 18.12.1975. The first partner has the personal tail 15-20-5 and centre 10, the second 21-10-7 and centre 14. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal charts, reduced to 22 or less:

The centre of this couple is 10 + 14 = 24 → 6, The Lovers: it belongs to the 37% where choice sits at the centre and The Devil at the entry of the first partner's personal tail. "The couple's values" is The Hermit. It is recalculated from the couple's sums rather than added from the partners' values: the sum 3 + 15 would have given 18, The Moon. Across all such couples The Hermit stands in the values for 54.1% and The Moon for 45.9%. In this example The Hermit also stands on the point "Attitude to material things": 5 + 22 = 27 → 9. Each role is read on its own: at the entry silence is a wish, in the values it is what the union exists for, in daily life it is unhurriedness and a reserve put by.

The middle of the couple's tail is not recalculated from its ends. In a personal chart the middle of the tail is the sum of the ends, and here that would be 9 + 12 = 21, The World. For a couple it is added from the partners' middles: 20 + 10 or 22 + 8 — both times 30, that is 3. Neither partner brings The Empress into the middle: she appears only between them.

As a personal tail, 9-3-12 does not occur for any date of birth. In a personal chart the entry M equals the main task D plus the centre. For the entry to be 9 with a main task of 12, the centre would have to be 15 (12 + 15 = 27 → 9), and no person has that centre. This tail exists only for two. It occurs in roughly one couple in 568 (0.176%), 77th place among the 97 couple tails.

sections.h2: The same cards in the order 9-12-3
paragraphs: The couple tail 9-12-3 is made of the same cards, but The Hanged Man stands in its middle and The Empress in the main task: the couple gets stuck along the way and learns to make things grow, and that tail is seven and a half times more common (1.334% of couples). In 9-3-12 it is the other way round: along the way things grow by themselves, and what has to be learned is not to hang in what has grown.

sections.h2: The strong version: a flower transplanted with its roots
paragraphs: The novel came out in 1809, three years after the most talked-about wedding in Weimar. In July 1788, in the park on the Ilm, a 23-year-old named Christiane Vulpius came up to Goethe with a petition for her brother. They lived together unmarried for eighteen years, and Weimar society did not accept their union. In October 1806, after the battle of Jena, French soldiers plundered the town, and Christiane stood in their way in Goethe's house. On 19 October the two were married in the sacristy of St James's Church. Lisovskaya writes of couples with The Hanged Man that they take a long time to enter a relationship and need a push from outside to marry. Here the push was a war.

In 1813, for the twenty-fifth anniversary of their meeting, Goethe wrote Christiane the poem "Gefunden" — "Found". It looks very simple, yet its five stanzas run through the whole 9-3-12 tail in its strong version. Here it is in full, in our own literal translation:

"I walked in the wood just by myself, and to seek nothing — that was my mind. In the shade I saw a little flower, shining like stars, lovely as little eyes. I wanted to pick it, and it said softly: am I to be broken only to wilt? I dug it out with all its little roots, carried it to the garden by the pretty house and planted it again in a quiet place. Now it keeps branching and blooms on."

The first stanza is The Hermit at his best: alone, and seeking nothing. The third is The Hanged Man's question: am I to be broken only to wilt? This is the sacrifice that kills. The answer is neither to pick it nor to leave it, but to dig it out with all its roots and transplant it. The last lines are The Empress: a garden by the house and a flower that "keeps branching". And "a quiet place" brings The Hermit back, only now the quiet does not shut anything off; it lets things grow.

The novel begins with grafting: Edward sets cut shoots on other young stems. The poem ends with transplanting, roots and all. These are two ways of joining one life to another. Grafting takes a shoot from someone without its roots and makes it grow on one's own stem. Transplanting takes the whole person — with their past, their family, their habits. A couple's tail is built like a transplant: it is made of two personal tails, and each partner brings their own roots into it. This is our reading, not a statement from the books, but for 9-3-12 it fits: **this couple's garden grows when both are transplanted whole rather than one grafted onto the other.**

ul: **Opening the book.** Silence for two is a strength as long as nothing unsaid is stored in it. From time to time, talk not about tasks but about what each is carrying inside right now.

**Asking every new undertaking what it is filling.** A house, renovations, a child, a business, a guest — The Empress is generous with all of them. The question is not "do we need this?" but "is this replacing a conversation?"
**Not making sacrifices nobody asked for.** A refusal made for the family's sake is worth discussing beforehand, not remembering afterwards, when one already wants to be repaid for it.
**Not waiting for a sign.** A glass, a coincidence of dates, "it will sort itself out" — in Goethe all of this leads to disaster. A decision is made by two, and out loud.
**Turning the view upside down.** A useful question for a couple with The Hanged Man: how does our garden look through the eyes of the one who lives in it, rather than the one who built it?

**9 · The Hermit — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: quiet, a world of its own, conversation without witnesses. The same wish can turn into resistance once the quiet no longer shuts out the world but shuts the two off from each other.

**3 · The Empress — middle of the task.** How the couple lives the path: building, planting, furnishing, raising. Abundance fills the space the two have fenced off for themselves, sometimes faster than they manage to talk about it.

**12 · The Hanged Man — main task.** What the couple has to learn: not to live in suspension, not to sacrifice in silence and not to wait for fate to decide for both. The Hanged Man can turn his view upside down, and that is his way out.

intro: Goethe wrote this story more than two hundred years ago. His novel Die Wahlverwandtschaften (Elective Affinities, 1809) opens in a nursery garden: a husband is grafting cuttings onto young trees while his wife finishes a moss hut on a rock. A few pages later he asks her whether everything they have made in the garden and the park is "only for a pair of hermits". What follows is an investigation: what is written in the three cards, in the books of Waite and Wen, and in the numbers of the tail itself.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 9-3-12 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: The couple enters its task wanting to be alone together (The Hermit), lives it through what it grows together — a home, children, a shared business (The Empress) — and its main task is not to hang in what has grown: not to spend years waiting and not to sacrifice in silence (The Hanged Man). It describes the couple's task, not a prediction of events.

faq.q: Why can a single person never have the 9-3-12 tail?
faq.a: In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre. A main task of 12 with an entry of 9 needs a centre of 15, and no date of birth gives a person The Devil at the centre. Besides, the middle of a personal tail equals the sum of its ends, and here 9 + 12 would give 21. The 9-3-12 tail is possible only in a couple's chart.

faq.q: Is the 9-3-12 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail shows what the couple is learning, not how the union will end. The same three cards also describe the strong version: a silence that lets things grow, a generous shared home and the ability to look at a situation from the other side in good time and make a decision.

faq.q: What do The Devil or The Lovers at the centre of such a couple mean?
faq.a: The centre is the atmosphere inside the couple. If the personal tails 3-22-19 and 6-8-20 meet, The Devil is always at the centre: the theme of an attraction that is hard to give up. If 15-20-5 and 21-10-7 meet, it is always The Lovers: the theme of choice. In both cases the other card stands at the entry of one partner's personal tail.

report: The Hanged Man in this couple's main task hangs not from a gallows but from a living tree. Waite is careful to point it out: "the tree of sacrifice is living wood, with leaves thereon", and the figure as a whole "suggests life in suspension, but life and not death". Where the living tree in the 9-3-12 tail comes from is clear from the other two cards. The Hermit at the entry is the wish to shut out the world and be alone together. The Empress in the middle is everything the two plant and raise in that solitude. The Hanged Man's tree grew in their own garden.

report.h3: A novel that opens with a question about hermits

report: Goethe wrote this story in 1809. Elective Affinities begins on an estate where Edward and Charlotte, married late after a long separation, have decided to live "merely that we might have our own lives to ourselves". In the moss hut on the rock Charlotte says it is large enough for the two of them. Edward wants to invite a friend to stay, Charlotte is against it, and he asks: **"All the work we have done — I in the garden, you in the park — is it all only for a pair of hermits?"** She answers with a premonition: she has seen husbands and wives "whose whole moral condition has been inverted" by the arrival of a third person. The man turned upside down is the twelfth card. The first chapter runs through the whole tail: two hermits, their garden and a foreboding of the overturn.

The novel is a mirror, not a forecast. In Goethe, the emptiness between two people is filled by people. The tail promises the couple neither a third nor a fourth. In real couples the emptiness is more often filled by things to do: renovations, a country house, children, work. The mechanism is the same.

report.h3: A silence for two and a silence for each

report: The Hermit at the entry is a common language of silence. A couple with this tail is happy together, does not much need guests, lets friends hear the news after the fact and shows love in deeds. But inside each partner there is a silence of their own as well. Edward flares up when Charlotte glances at his page: "When anybody looks over my book, I always feel as if I were being torn in two."

The same wish easily becomes resistance. The hut built for the two of them soon holds four, and later it becomes the place Charlotte runs to alone — Goethe calls it "the little hermitage". Solitude for two has become solitude for one. This is how the weak entry looks: the unsaid gets stored in the shared silence — hurt, tiredness, doubt.

The Empress in the middle is the couple's path through growth. In the novel both guests are let in by the household: the Captain comes to survey the estate and run the works, Ottilie to replace the departing housekeeper. From then on the novel turns into a book about landscape gardening: a house on the hill, three ponds joined into one lake, though the Captain thinks it "in more than one sense, a very questionable proceeding". For Wen, The Empress is the card of fruition that "might also be a foreshadowing of unintended or unanticipated consequences affecting that fruition". The lake made for the sake of the view becomes, in Goethe, the scene of the great disaster.

At the christening of Edward and Charlotte's son, Ottilie sees her own eyes in the baby's face, and the family friend sees the Captain's features. The child resembles the people his parents thought about and kept silent about. **The unsaid grows into what the two create together** — in a real couple not in children, but in the tone of the house, in daily life, in where the strength and money go. A weak Empress is building work that never ends, because while it goes on nobody has to talk about the main thing.

The second part of the novel is suspension from start to finish. Edward goes off to war, resolving to "put myself in the place of this glass", the glass that did not break at the foundation-stone ceremony. Charlotte waits and gives up her own feeling. Ottilie takes a vow of silence and admits she has observed her promise "too literally". The marriage is neither lived nor dissolved. It hangs. At the end Edward says: "genius is required for everything; for martyrdom as well as the rest." Wen, describing the reversed Hanged Man, warns of the same thing: "not to confuse martyrdom with selfishness".

In life it is more ordinary. She does not go to her class reunion "because there's so much to do at home". He turns down a job in another city "because of the family". Nobody asked for these sacrifices, and a few years later they are presented for payment — as reproach, as tiredness, as silence at dinner. The most exact words are spoken by Charlotte when it is already too late: "I ought to have made up my mind to it before." **The Hanged Man in the main task is waiting for a sign.** What the couple has to learn is not patience but how to stop hanging.

The way out is written in the same book. Man, Charlotte says, "is raised very many steps above these elements", and "will do well to turn back again into himself" before calling what happens choice or fate. At the end she breaks off her own words about destiny: "It is but my own desire, my own purpose… which destiny is again bringing in my way." This is The Hermit in his strong form — solitude in order to think, not in order to hide. And The Hanged Man in his strong form: the same garden seen from the other side.

Four years after the novel Goethe wrote his wife, Christiane Vulpius, the poem "Found". He walks in the wood just by himself, seeking nothing. He sees a flower and wants to pick it, and the flower asks: am I to be broken only to wilt? So he digs it out "with all its little roots", carries it to the garden by the house, plants it in a quiet place, and the flower "keeps branching and blooms on". This is the 9-3-12 tail in its strong version: silence, the question of sacrifice and a garden that grows.

The novel began with grafting: Edward sets cut shoots on other stems. The poem ends with transplanting, roots and all. Grafting takes a shoot from someone and makes it grow on one's own stem. Transplanting takes the whole person, with their past and their habits. This is our reading, but for a couple with this tail it fits: **the garden grows when both are transplanted whole rather than one grafted onto the other.** The rest is simple: open the book to each other, ask every new undertaking whether it is replacing a conversation, make no sacrifices nobody asked for, and decide together and out loud instead of waiting for a sign.

unit.title: Not hanging in your own garden

captions.M: Shut out the world together and guard your shared quiet
captions.N: Grow a home and shared work without letting it replace talk
captions.D: Stop hanging while you wait for a sign, and decide out loud

unit.meaning: Your task is not to hang in what you have grown together: make no silent sacrifices and decide out loud, not by a sign.
